content: In the United States, graduates of chiropractic schools earn the degree of Doctor of Chiropractic (DC). They are referred to as doctors and are eligible to apply for licensure in all jurisdictions. The Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE) establishes minimum standards for chiropractic colleges, although additional requirements may vary depending on the jurisdiction where a chiropractor intends to practice. All 19 chiropractic institutions in the U.S. are accredited by the CCE. In 1991, the University of Bridgeport established its College of Chiropractic, becoming the first chiropractic school in the U.S. affiliated with a university. While many students enter chiropractic school with a bachelor's degree, as of 2005, only one chiropractic college required a bachelor's degree for admission. Common prerequisite courses include psychology, biology, organic and inorganic chemistry, and physics. Other medical courses typically required include anatomy, embryology, physiology, microbiology, diagnosis, neurology, radiology, orthopedics, obstetrics/gynecology, histology, and pathology. Chiropractic programs require at least 4,200 hours of combined classroom, laboratory, and clinical training. The final two years emphasize spinal manipulation and adjustment techniques, as well as clinical experience in physical and laboratory diagnosis, orthopedics, neurology, geriatrics, physiotherapy, and nutrition. To obtain licensure, graduates must pass four examinations administered by the National Board of Chiropractic Examiners and meet state-specific requirements. Most state boards require at least two years of undergraduate education, and an increasing number require a four-year bachelor's degree. All U.S. licensing boards mandate completion of a four-year program at an accredited chiropractic college leading to the DC degree. Once licensed, most states require chiropractors to complete 12–50 hours of continuing education annually. Chiropractic colleges also offer postdoctoral training in specialties such as neurology, orthopedics, sports injuries, nutrition, rehabilitation, industrial consulting, radiology, family practice, pediatrics, and applied chiropractic sciences. Chiropractors who complete such training may take exams to achieve diplomate status in specific specialties, including orthopedics, neurology, and radiology. In Canada, there are two chiropractic schools: the Canadian Memorial Chiropractic College (CMCC) in Toronto, Ontario, and the Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières (UQTR) in Quebec. Both programs are fully accredited by the Council on Chiropractic Education of Canada. Canadian chiropractic students undergo a curriculum similar to that of other doctoral-level healthcare professionals, such as medicine, optometry, and dentistry, with comparable entrance requirements. Students must complete at least three years of university education before being eligible for admission to the CMCC Doctorate of Chiropractic program. Approximately 90% of CMCC students have completed a baccalaureate or graduate degree prior to admission. The CMCC program is privately funded and requires four years of full-time study, including a 12-month clinical internship. Both the CMCC and UQTR programs include courses in anatomy, neuroanatomy, neurodiagnosis, neuroscience, biochemistry, physiology, orthopedics, diagnosis, symptomatology, laboratory diagnosis, embryology, chiropractic principles, radiology, immunology, microbiology, pathology, clinical nutrition, and other basic and clinical medical sciences. The psychomotor department at CMCC teaches the diversified technique for spinal manipulative therapy and formally introduced soft tissue techniques in 2006. Canadian chiropractic schools emphasize an evidence-based medicine paradigm rather than the traditional vertebral subluxation model. Chiropractors in Canada are considered primary care providers for neuromusculoskeletal conditions, assessing, diagnosing, and treating biomechanical dysfunctions of the neuromusculoskeletal system. They may also prescribe corrective exercises, provide nutritional recommendations, and promote healthy lifestyle practices. Depending on the province, chiropractors may order diagnostic imaging such as X-rays, MRIs, CT scans, and ultrasounds. The Canadian Chiropractic Examining Board requires all candidates to complete a 12-month clinical internship and pass three examinations during their fourth year of study to obtain licensure. Canadian accreditation standards are stricter than those in the United States, and admission requirements for the Doctorate of Chiropractic program are the most rigorous in North America. In Australia, chiropractic education is offered at three public universities: RMIT University in Melbourne, Murdoch University in Perth, and Macquarie University in Sydney. RMIT and Macquarie programs award a master's degree, while Murdoch University offers a double bachelor's degree. These qualifications are necessary for registration with state regulatory boards. In the United Kingdom, there are three chiropractic colleges recognized by the General Chiropractic Council (GCC), the statutory governmental body responsible for chiropractic regulation. These colleges are the Anglo-European College of Chiropractic (AECC), accredited by Bournemouth University; the McTimoney College of Chiropractic (MCC), accredited by the University of Wales; and the Welsh Institute of Chiropractic (WIOC), a faculty of the University of South Wales. AECC graduates earn an undergraduate master's degree (MChiro), while MCC and WIOC graduates earn a BSc (Hons) in Chiropractic. Registration with the GCC is a legal requirement for all chiropractors practicing in the UK. In South Africa, chiropractic education is offered at the Durban University of Technology and the University of Johannesburg. Both institutions provide six-year full-time programs leading to a Master of Technology (MTech) in Chiropractic. Chiropractors must register with the Allied Health Professions Council of South Africa (AHPCSA) to practice legally. Membership in the Chiropractic Association of South Africa (CASA) is voluntary. Continuing professional development (CPD) is not mandatory for maintaining registration with the AHPCSA, but chiropractors must pay annual registration fees. The Federation of Chiropractic Licensing Boards (FCLB) is a coalition of all 50 U.S. state licensing boards, the District of Columbia, several Canadian provinces, and U.S. territories. Its mission is to protect the public and support member boards by promoting excellence in chiropractic regulation. Chiropractic schools worldwide vary significantly in their entry criteria, program structure, teaching methods, and curriculum. The Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE-USA) is the accrediting agency for chiropractic programs in the United States, ensuring the quality of chiropractic education through accreditation standards, educational improvement, and public information.
